standard.title: Develop historical questions
standard.description: develop historical questions about the past to inform historical inquiry
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can develop questions about objects, people, places, and events in the past and present (AC9HS6S01). They have not yet distinguished historical inquiry questions from general questions — specifically the disciplinary requirements of historical questions: they must be investigable using evidence, focused on historical significance, causation, continuity/change, or perspective, and they must be open enough to require analysis rather than simple recall.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop historical questions that can inform historical inquiry — questions that are focused on historically significant issues, investigable using historical evidence, and framed around historical concepts such as causation, continuity and change, perspective, or significance.

nodes.label: What makes a question historical?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a general question about the past and a historical inquiry question, and explain what makes a question suitable for historical inquiry — investigable using evidence, focused on historical significance or causation.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the difference between a recall question ('When did X happen?') and a historical inquiry question ('Why did X happen?' or 'How did X change?'), and explain why the inquiry question is more useful for historical investigation.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the characteristics of a historical inquiry question — that it must be investigable using evidence, focused on historical significance, causation, continuity/change, or perspective, and open enough to require analysis. Distinguish these from recall questions, opinion questions, and questions that cannot be answered by historical evidence.
wider: Examine how the framing of a question shapes what evidence is needed and what conclusions are possible — comparing how differently framed questions about the same event would lead to different investigations.

Investigate the concept of historical significance and how it can be operationalised as a question — what makes something worth investigating historically, and how students can ask questions that focus on significance.

Explore how historians generate inquiry questions — from curiosity, from gaps in existing knowledge, from new evidence — and examine published historical inquiries to identify the questions that drove them.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish historical inquiry questions from recall questions will produce recall questions when applying concept frames in N2 — the concept frames are applied correctly only if students understand what makes a question genuinely investigable.

response_modes.reason: The concept of a 'historical inquiry question' as distinct from a general question requires explicit reasoning about what history as a discipline is trying to do. Students need the distinction made explicit — recall vs analysis; answerable by fact vs requiring evidence-based argument — before they can apply it reliably. Without this scaffold, students produce recall or opinion questions rather than inquiry questions.

success_criteria: Correctly distinguishes a historical inquiry question from a recall or opinion question.
Identifies at least two characteristics of a good historical inquiry question (investigable, focused on causation/change/significance/perspective).
Can sort a given set of questions into 'suitable for historical inquiry' and 'not suitable', with reasons.

nodes.label: Developing questions using historical concepts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop historical inquiry questions using the key historical concepts — causation, continuity and change, perspective, and significance — as question frames.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop at least two historical inquiry questions using different historical concept frames (e.g. one causation question and one continuity/change question) about the same topic.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a range of historical inquiry questions using the key historical concept frames — causation ('Why did...?', 'What caused...?'), continuity and change ('How did... change/continue?'), perspective ('How did... experience/view...?'), and significance ('Why is... historically significant?') — applied to topics from the K-strand content.
wider: Examine how changing the concept frame changes the investigation — taking the same historical topic and developing four different questions (causation, change, perspective, significance) to explore how each would lead to a different inquiry.

Investigate how complex historical questions combine multiple concept frames — 'Why did the Roman Empire fall and what continued after its decline?' combines causation and continuity/change — and why complex questions sometimes produce richer inquiries.

Explore how the questions historians actually ask have changed over time — from 'great men' questions to social history questions to cultural history questions — as evidence that what counts as a historical question is itself historically situated.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who revert to recall questions under independent practice cannot produce the appropriately scoped questions in N3 — N3 builds directly on reliable question formulation with concept frames, and fluency with those frames is the prerequisite.

response_modes.reason: Applying historical concept frames to generate questions is a skill requiring practice and precision. Students commonly revert to recall or opinion questions when working independently, even after understanding the concept distinction. Regular practice — developing questions across different frames, on different topics, checking against criteria — is the investment that builds reliable question formulation.

success_criteria: Develops at least two historical inquiry questions using different concept frames.
Questions are genuinely investigable using historical evidence — not answerable by simple recall.
Correctly identifies which historical concept (causation, change, perspective, significance) each question draws on.

nodes.label: Questions that inform inquiry — scope and focus
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop historical questions that are appropriately scoped for inquiry — not so broad as to be unanswerable and not so narrow as to require only recall — and explain how their question would guide the selection of evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a historical inquiry question and explain in basic terms what types of evidence would be needed to investigate it.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a historical inquiry question that is appropriately scoped for the available evidence, explain what types of evidence would be needed to investigate it, and demonstrate awareness of how the question's scope (breadth, time period, focus) shapes what counts as a relevant answer.
wider: Refine a broad question into a more focused, investigable form — demonstrating the process of moving from initial curiosity to a researchable question — and explain what was gained and lost in the refinement.
Develop a set of sub-questions that break a complex inquiry question into manageable components, and explain how each sub-question contributes to answering the main question.
Examine how historians phrase their central questions in published works, and analyse what makes those questions effective as guides for inquiry.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the concept of a historical question (Node 1) and the skill of generating questions using concept frames (Node 2) into the descriptor's full demand — developing questions that genuinely inform inquiry. Students must coordinate the disciplinary requirements of historical questions with appropriate scope and evidence awareness, producing questions that are both historically focused and practically investigable.

success_criteria: Develops a historical inquiry question that is appropriately scoped — investigable, not a simple recall or overly broad question.
Identifies what types of evidence would be needed to investigate the question.
Explains how the question would guide the investigation — what it would require the student to look for.
